articles.title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
articles.summary: The comedian and Celebrity Traitors win big - see a full list of winners and nominees from the 26th edition of the awards.
articles.body:
You can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this article

Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian.

The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award.

Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends.

He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?"

Carr was right - Mrs Brown's Boys went on to win the Comedy prize. But the night was just beginning.

The Celebrity Traitors favourite had predicted there would be "ugly crying" if he did take home a prize - and he stayed true to his word as he accepted the Special Recognition award, the only category not voted for by the public.

Carr told BBC News that being part of The Celebrity Traitors had brought him a level of attention he had never experienced before.

"I've never had popularity like it," he said, describing the show as a "phenomenon".

Carr had more reason to celebrate when The Celebrity Traitors beat the original version of the show to win the Reality Competition prize.

His co-star, singer Charlotte Church, praised the show's final, which attracted 15 million viewers within seven days, describing it as a "beautiful vignette of male tenderness and emotional expression".

"Alan, Nick (Mohammed) and David (Olusoga), you were just absolutely sublime," she added.

Sir David Attenborough wins an NTA at 100

Another big win went to Sir David Attenborough, who was named Best Presenter in his 100th birthday year, beating popular duo Ant and Dec, whose 23-year winning streak was broken by Gary Lineker last year.

While not in attendance, Attenborough's long-time collaborator Mark Brownlow accepted the award on his behalf and shared a message from the broadcaster urging people to help protect the planet.

"Humanity has always needed the natural world for all the practicalities of life and for our mental wellbeing," Attenborough wrote. "Now the natural world needs us too: surely we must not ignore that simple fact."

Clarkson's Farm won an NTA for the second year running, taking the inaugural Celebrity-Led Reality Docuseries award.

The new category also featured shows from Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash, Tyson Fury, Kelvin Fletcher, and Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse.

Celebrity-led programmes still featured in the Authored Documentary category, with documentaries from Olympian Sir Chris Hoy, former Little Mix singer Jesy Nelson, and Sharon Osbourne's film about her late husband Ozzy among the nominees.

Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet, their daughter Kelly Osbourne said her family were "honoured" that the documentary about her father had been nominated, describing it as a "tragic but beautiful story".

She said she had spoken to her mother Sharon just before arriving at the ceremony: "We are so close. I was on the phone with her before I got out of the car."

In the end, the public chose Our Girls: The Southport Families. The BBC programme followed the families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, who were murdered at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in 2024.

Accepting the award, Elsie's mother Jenni Stancombe told the audience: "We never expected to be stood up here, so I don't know what to say.

"We know you didn't vote for us, you voted for our three girls."

In the drama categories, Vicky McClure won Best Drama Performance for her role in crime thriller Trigger Point, from the first all-female shortlist in the category's history.

She told BBC News in the winners' room: "Over the years it has not been our space, and here we are dominating that category.

"I feel honoured to be amongst those wonderful women."

Among those nominated alongside McClure was Sheridan Smith for her portrayal of campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law.

While Smith missed out on the individual prize, I Fought The Law went on to win New Drama.

Norton dusts off his Swift-Kelce wedding suit

Away from the awards, nominee Graham Norton revealed his red carpet outfit had already had one high-profile outing this year.

"This is what I wore to Taylor Swift's wedding," he told BBC News.

Norton said guests had agreed not to reveal details of the celebrations. "I had a wonderful time and we all agreed by saying yes to going, we weren't going to blab about it."

Norton, who also featured in Swift's music video for Opalite earlier this year, said working with the singer showed him "what leadership is like at that level".

"It was such a happy set. Everyone was working as hard as they could for her," he said.

articles.title: US Supreme Court rejects Missouri bid to reactivate GOP-backed voting map
articles.summary: A separate federal court ruling, however, contradicts the Supreme Court judgement, leaving the map up in the air.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has declined to reinstate a Republican-backed congressional map in Missouri, leaving in place an older map for November’s midterm elections.

On Tuesday, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who handles emergency matters from Missouri, rejected the state’s request to put the new map into effect. He did not refer the case to the full nine-member court nor explain his decision.

The decision is a setback for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, which had backed the redistricting effort as part of a broader push to improve their electoral chances.

The new Republican-backed map would have given the party a better chance of winning an extra seat in the US House of Representatives by carving up Missouri’s Democratic-leaning 5th congressional district.

But the outcome of the legal battle remains unclear.

In the hours after Justice Kavanaugh’s decision, a federal court in Missouri temporarily blocked the older congressional map from being used.

That decision by US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump appointee, requires Missouri to use the new Republican-backed map for the November midterms.

His order will remain in effect for 14 days while courts consider the dispute. Opponents of the new map have already filed an appeal.

Tuesday’s contrasting court decisions are likely to boost confusion in Missouri, with less than two months to go before the midterm race.

The dispute centers on a congressional map approved by Missouri Republicans in 2025. Missouri joined several other right-leaning states, including Texas, in heeding Trump’s call to redraw their congressional districts to favour Republican candidates.

The new boundaries would have broken up the 5th congressional district, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver. The district includes much of Kansas City, but the new map would have seen parts of the older district shifted into neighbouring Republican-held districts.

Opponents of the partisan redistricting effort, however, gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures to force the new map to be put up for a vote.

That triggered the ongoing legal battle. Missouri’s Republican officials refused to accept the petition as legal, sparking a lawsuit.

The Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled last week that voters must approve the Republican-backed map in a statewide referendum before it can be used.

Kavanaugh’s decision on Tuesday would have allowed last week’s decision to stand. But Clark’s subsequent ruling has added another layer of uncertainty to the issue.

Also complicating the legal dynamics of the case is the fact that Missouri has already held its party primaries using the Republican-backed map.

Opponents of the map argue that Republican officials intentionally dismissed the referendum petition shortly before the primary, with no time to appeal.

Missouri’s Republican attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, argued that reverting to the older map would interfere with the election process, given that the primary was decided with the new map.

Hanaway also said the state “is prepared to follow and comply with” the Clark’s Tuesday order, which she said “binds the state to using” the new congressional districts.

At stake is Republican control over the US House. Republicans hold a narrow majority of 219 positions in the 435-seat chamber, including one right-leaning independent.

Democrats hold 214 seats, meaning the race for control of the chamber is likely to come down to a handful of elections.

As a result of Trump’s mid-decade redistricting push, Republicans improved their chances in roughly 16 districts across the country, including Cleaver’s seat in Missouri. Democrats, meanwhile, have gained an advantage in six districts.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial
articles.summary: The three jurors said after 40 hours, a lone male juror wouldn't agree with the rest of the panel to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.
articles.body:
Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial have made their first public remarks about the secretive deliberations and what led to their deadlock before the high-profile case ended in a mistrial.

Three female jurors - including the foreperson - told NBC the panel was ready to enter a verdict that Clancy was not guilty by way of insanity in the murder of her three children, but one juror would not agree.

The foreperson said the male juror "admitted he had reasonable doubt" in her criminal responsibility but wouldn't agree to a not guilty verdict.

Clancy has not denied the killings but her attorneys argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors argued she made a calculated decision.

Lindsay Clancy's lawyer hopes for deal with prosecutors after mistrial

What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ends in a mistrial?

The identities of the nine women and three men on the jury have not been made public and the judge banned any photographing or filming of them during the trial to retain their anonymity.

But in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose whether or not to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Jurors often choose to speak out - some even write books - after high-profile cases like that of Clancy.

The BBC, which was in the court during the case, has confirmed the three women who spoke with NBC were on the jury panel.

In the interview with the local Boston NBC affiliate NBC10, which aired on Tuesday, the jury foreperson - a retired fifth-grade teacher - called not being able to reach a verdict in the case "awful" and an "emotional roller coaster". A foreperson acts as a spokesperson for a jury in any US legal case, meaning they are the person delivering a verdict and sending notes to the judge on behalf of the 12-person panel.

She said the deliberations were difficult and filled with "lots of crying" and "lots of tears and then hugging".

"I was so sad, so sad that we couldn't come up with a verdict for Lindsay. It was so heartbreaking," she added.

Throughout the interview, the three women said the jury was in nearly unanimous agreement to enter their verdict but the holdout juror would not change his mind.

The foreperson said the lone juror "admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited".

She was halfway through filling out the verdict sheets when the holdout juror, who she said was a man, continued: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity," she says he told the panel.

The man in question has not come forward and has not responded to these comments.

The three jurors noted their deliberations led to fights and yelling, which at times could be heard through the walls.

Under Massachusetts law, there was no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility. Rather, it was on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon previously told the BBC.

"We weren't trying to figure out if she murdered the children. She did and she's admitted that," the foreperson explained in the interview with NBC. "We're trying to figure out - did she know right from wrong at that time."

The three jurors noted they didn't feel persuaded by the prosecution.

"Everything proved that she loved her children so she had to have snapped and not known what she was doing," the foreperson said.

Another juror, who does work for a government defence contractor, said the holdout juror had questions about what medication Clancy was on.

"We had the toxicology reports. We could see exactly the amounts," she said, adding that there were nurses on the jury who spoke about that. "He just completely disregarded the information that they gave," the juror added.

The third juror, a chef at a senior centre, said she found the prosecutors in the case to be "very, very harsh", adding: "They had no character witness in regard to Lindsay of being a bad mother."

Throughout the trial, prosecutors called dozens of witnesses, including several doctors, seeking to prove Clancy had made a calculated decision to murder her children in the basement of their Massachusetts home.

The grim case led to a series of dramatic twists and turns as the jury deliberated for nearly 40 hours over seven days to determine Clancy's fate. They signalled multiple times they were facing a deadlock - and at one point told the judge that one member of the panel was not following the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt.

The development led to Clancy's defence attorney requesting the holdout juror be removed from the panel - a request that was quickly denied - before the panel again said they could not come to a unanimous decision.

Judge William Sullivan then declared a mistrial on Friday.

The mistrial leaves both the case and Clancy's future uncertain, as prosecutors determine whether they want to take the case to trial a second time with a new jury.

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has since said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors so the case doesn't see a second trial.

The three jurors told NBC they hoped there wasn't a second trial - but if there is - all three said they plan to attend in support of Clancy.

How the Lindsay Clancy trial gripped America - and ultimately fell apart

articles.title: Gambian leader pledges halt to rolling blackouts as protests turn violent
articles.summary: Barrow pledges new power infrastructure, including a 24-megawatt plant, to tackle the worsening electricity crisis.
articles.body:
Gambian President Adama Barrow has said the country will boost energy supplies by next month, hoping to quell violent protests over prolonged power outages as the premier stands for re-election .

Protesters burned tyres and built barricades blocking traffic, demanding that Barrow resign, in The Gambia’s capital, Banjul, and nearby cities on Monday and Tuesday.

Police used tear gas to disperse crowds who gathered in multiple locations, including near Barrow’s residence and the National Water and Electricity Corporation (NAWEC) headquarters, which supplies the country’s electricity.

Barrow declared the outages an emergency and a “national security issue” during a visit to a NAWEC power station. In a national address, he announced that the government would install a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October.

“I know that the fans have stopped turning, children work in the dark, mothers throw away stale food, and the heat is unbearable by day and by night,” Barrow said.

The rolling blackouts are taking place during the West African country’s hot season and have lasted up to 48 hours in some places.

The Gambian president also announced an additional 50-megawatt solar power plant that would begin construction soon.

NAWEC Managing Director Gallo said the prolonged electricity cuts were in part due to climate change and the US-Israel war on Iran. The electricity provider, in a statement released in August, also claimed that it was experiencing an “unforeseen surge” in demand due to high temperatures.

The blackouts come just months ahead of the December presidential election, in which Barrow is running for a third term .

articles.title: Five baby orangutans found abandoned in Odisha forest during routine patrolling by forest officials: How did the non- native species get there?
articles.summary: Animals & Pets News: A group of young orangutans was found abandoned in a stretch of forest in Odisha, but what made this discovery unusual is that these animals belong no.
articles.body: A group of young orangutans was found abandoned in a stretch of forest in Odisha, but what made this discovery unusual is that these animals belong nowhere near India's east coast.Orangutans are large, tree-dwelling intelligent apes with reddish-brown fur. They're found only in the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, split between Indonesia and Malaysia, and are not native to India.Orangutans are native to Southeast Asia, specifically the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they have lived for millions of years. Their ancestors were part of a wider group of ancient great apes that once spread across Asia and Europe. Today, three recognized orangutan species remain: the Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli orangutan. They are the only great apes naturally found in Asia. The name “orangutan” comes from Malay and Indonesian words meaning “person of the forest.” Their survival is closely tied to tropical rainforests, where they spend much of their lives in trees and feed mainly on fruits, leaves and other vegetation.Let’s dig in to find out what exactly happened and how they got there.5 baby orangutans found abandoned in Odisha’s forest during a routine forest patrolOn Tuesday, September 8, 2026, the Odisha Forest Department rescued five young orangutans that had been abandoned in a casuarina plantation in the Udayapur-Talsari forest area of Balasore district. Forest staff found the animals during a routine patrol in the Udayapur section of the Jaleswar Range.According to The Hindu report, the animals, aged between six months and a year, comprise three males and two females. Regional Chief Conservator of Forests Prakash Chand Gogineni confirmed the numbers directly, saying, according to Gogineni, "We have rescued all of them. Of the five, three are male, and two are female."What makes this case unusual is that orangutans have no natural presence in India at all. They're found only in the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia, which means these animals had to have been brought into the country, almost certainly illegally.It is a suspected case of illegal smugglingGogineni suspects the abandonment was linked to a smuggling attempt gone wrong, saying, according to him, "It appears to be a botched-up transit operation." He added that the animals seem to have been brought to the area and then simply left behind in the plantation.Furthermore, DFO, Balasore, Indalkar Pratik Prakash told ANI, "They were small and not moving much, but were active and were provided with food. They were rescued and brought to the section office. We estimate that they may have been released there last night or early this morning. While smuggling remains a possibility, there is no conclusive evidence yet. Since their natural habitat is tropical rainforests, they could not have migrated there naturally, indicating possible human intervention. Investigations are underway to determine how they arrived there... "At this stage, officials don't yet know exactly where the orangutans entered the country or who was responsible. Gogineni said the department has no leads yet on the point of entry along the coast, and confirmed that a case is being registered under the Wildlife Protection Act while the investigation moves forward.Odisha's Forest and Environment Minister, Ganesh Ram Singhkhuntia, said a separate team has been sent to the Badapai–Ranakatha area specifically to piece together how the animals ended up there and to identify anyone who might be involved, adding that the matter remains under active investigation.The rescued orangutans have undergone a full medical check-up and are safeThe rescued orangutans, showing no visible injuries, have been moved to Nandankanan Zoological Park for a full medical check-up. The Forest and Wildlife Department has also alerted its coastal divisions and asked them to check for any other orangutans that may have been abandoned nearby, in case this wasn't an isolated incident.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Thousands protest in Germany as far-right AfD eyes first state government since the Nazi Party
articles.summary: Europe News: Thousands of people took to the streets across Germany after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) recorded its strongest-ever result in a state.
articles.body: Thousands of people took to the streets across Germany after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) recorded its strongest-ever result in a state election, raising fears that the party could make further gains in upcoming polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.The protests followed the AfD's victory in Sunday's election in Saxony-Anhalt, where it won nearly 44% of the vote and secured 39 of the 83 seats in the state legislature. While the party fell short of the majority needed to govern on its own, it is seeking support from lawmakers from other parties to form what would be Germany's first far-right state government since the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP), or Nazi Party, ruled the country.In Berlin, demonstrators gathered around the Brandenburg Gate for a pro-democracy rally opposing the AfD. Police estimated the crowd at about 5,000, while organisers said more than 14,000 people attended. Protests were also reported in Potsdam, Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt and Halberstadt.The rallies reflected growing concern over the AfD's electoral momentum. Protesters carried signs opposing racism and fascism, while speakers urged voters not to become resigned after the Saxony-Anhalt result.Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, described the result as a “disgrace” and warned against accepting the prospect of an AfD-led government in silence.The election has also put pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Merz ruled out cooperation with the AfD but acknowledged that the result had shaken his party “to its very foundations”. He rejected suggestions that he should resign, saying he would continue with his government's reform programme.The AfD's rise is now being watched closely ahead of state elections scheduled for September 20. The party is leading voter-intention polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania at around 35%, although the centre-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) has narrowed the gap after recovering support in recent months. Berlin's contest is even more fragmented, with the CDU holding only a narrow lead over the Left party and AfD.Germany's long-standing political “firewall” against the AfD is also facing renewed scrutiny. The country's mainstream parties have traditionally refused to cooperate with the party, while the AfD has criticised the policy as undemocratic. The populist-left BSW, however, has signalled that it could work with the AfD, particularly on issues including migration and Germany's policy towards Russia.The AfD has been classified as right-wing extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency in Saxony-Anhalt, a designation the party rejects. Its national leadership has portrayed the Saxony-Anhalt result as a major breakthrough, with co-leader Alice Weidel saying the party would aim for at least 40% in Germany's next national election in 2029.Meanwhile, the result has drawn concern beyond Germany. French finance minister Roland Lescure described the AfD's success as a “very, very worrying signal”, saying Europe was facing a broader populist challenge.The latest rallies are part of a broader mobilisation against the AfD’s anti-immigration and nationalist agenda, which has repeatedly drawn protests over its proposals to tighten migration rules and pursue deportations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Festivals are inclusive': Amruta Fadnavis opposes VHP call to bar Muslims from Navratri events
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Amruta Fadnavis, wife of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis, said there was nothing wrong with Muslims participating in Navratri .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Amruta Fadnavis, wife of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis, said there was nothing wrong with Muslims participating in Navratri and other festivals, after the Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP) called for Muslims to be barred from the upcoming Navratri festivities, a demand endorsed by state minister Nitesh Rane.“Festivals are inclusive, and there is nothing wrong with a Muslim person attending the celebrations. If a Muslim also comes and enjoys the festival properly, I do not see anything wrong with it,” Amruta Fadnavis told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday, PTI reported.Her remarks came in response to a question on Rane’s comments. On Monday, Rane, a BJP colleague of Devendra Fadnavis, backed the VHP, alleging that cases of “love jihad” tend to increase during such festivals. He also called for attendees to undergo identity checks and recite the Hanuman Chalisa before being allowed entry to Navratri events.“Love jihad” is a term used by right-wing activists to allege that Muslim men lure women, mostly from the Hindu community, into relationships with the aim of converting them to Islam.Last week, the VHP announced that Muslims would not be allowed to enter ‘garba’ and ‘dandiya’ venues across Maharashtra during Navratri, which begins on October 11.The VHP has also issued “guidelines” for organisers to verify participants’ identities at Navratri ‘garba’ and ‘dandiya’ events by checking their Aadhaar cards and applying ‘tilak’ on their foreheads.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Data shows Amazon jet’s key braking systems did not deploy during deadly Miami crash: NTSB
articles.summary: The NTSB said the cargo jet’s wheel brakes were applied, but its speed brakes and thrust reversers did not deploy, according to available data.
articles.body: Authorities on Tuesday said key braking systems did not deploy during Sunday’s deadly plane crash after an Amazon cargo jet overran the runway at Miami International Airport and struck two vehicles, killing five people. While the aircraft’s wheel brakes were applied, available data indicates that the speed brakes and thrust reversers did not, according to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). There was "no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed," Chihoon Shin, the NTSB investigator in charge, said. Shin said investigators plan to interview the pilots involved, adding that officials are not yet going to speculate about what should have happened during the landing. AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY AND STRIKES 'MULTIPLE' VEHICLES; 5 DEAD, 5 INJURED "When we analyze the full list of parameters, we'll have a better idea of the aircraft's performance during this landing. Was it normal? Was it not? And what was working and what was not. So I'm not going to speculate on what should have been right now," he said. "What we need to do is talk to the crew and get their account to understand how they're manipulating the controls in order to get a better understanding of the situation," he added. "That's something that we need a complete understanding of." VICTIMS IDENTIFIED IN FATAL AMAZON CARGO JET CRASH AT MIAMI AIRPORT While officials did not identify the pilots involved, NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the captain was 55 years old and had 7,145 flight hours, according to his latest Class 1 medical certificate dated March 31, 2026. The first officer was 37 years old and had 2,655 flight hours, according to his Class 1 medical certificate dated April 13, 2026, she said. Officials confirmed that no hazardous materials were on board and said most of the cargo consisted of contact lenses. articles.title: Cluster munitions kill, wound over 1,000 globally in 2025
articles.summary: The 1,063 global casualties in 2025 one of the highest annual tolls on record, a report has found.
articles.body:
Cluster munitions have killed or injured at least 1,063 people in 2025, one of the highest annual tolls on record, according to a report produced by a global network of researchers.

Most casualties were civilians, including at least 34 children, the Cluster Munition Coalition’s annual report said on Tuesday. Deaths and injuries were recorded in Afghanistan, Cambodia, Iraq, Laos, Lebanon, Myanmar, Russia, Syria and Ukraine.

Ukraine had the highest number of recorded casualties for the fourth consecutive year in 2025, accounting for 87 percent of the global total.

The actual number is likely higher as many casualties go unreported, the report said. The highest toll was recorded in 2022, 1,172, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine that year.

Cluster munitions consist of small compartments that disperse small explosives indiscriminately, posing significant danger to civilian populations. Explosives can remain undetonated long after they are dispersed.

Adopted during the Oslo Process, the Convention on Cluster Munitions took effect in 2010 after Norway and several other countries aimed to create an international treaty to protect civilians from the controversial explosive weapons.

The convention prohibits the use, production, and collection of cluster munitions. The treaty has 112 states parties and 12 signatories. Lithuania is the first and only country to withdraw from the convention in March.

The Cluster Munition Coalition reported that cluster munitions were used by Iran, Myanmar, Russia, Thailand, Ukraine, and Mali, which is a party to the convention.

The report added that while it was not able to verify the claims, there were reports of use by Israel and the US in Iran, by Pakistan in Afghanistan, by Houthi forces in Israel, and by Israel in Lebanon.

Evidence of new production was found in China, India, Israel, Myanmar, North Korea, Poland, Romania, Russia, and South Korea. The report added that evidence suggests that the US plans new production of cluster munitions in the future.

The US and Russia voted against an annual resolution promoting the convention in the United Nations General Assembly in December, for the first time since it was introduced.

The report said the cuts in US foreign assistance last year disrupted clearance of cluster munition remnants, which resulted in the death and injury of at least 117 people in 2025.

articles.title: Ukraine’s battlefield optimism is ebbing as Russia threatens its ‘fortress belt’
articles.summary: Iryna Rybakova is horribly aware that the front line is inching toward Kramatorsk. Having served in eastern Ukraine for several years, she has watched her units being pushed from one strategic hub after another. But she said the past few weeks have been “insane.”
articles.body: Iryna Rybakova is horribly aware that the front line is inching toward Kramatorsk. Having served in eastern Ukraine for several years, she has watched her units being pushed from one strategic hub after another. But she said the past few weeks have been “insane.” The city remains one of Ukraine’s last strongholds in the Donbas region, but the Russians are getting dangerously close. Nearly all of the city’s bridges have been destroyed, and barrages of guided bombs and drones are now a daily reality. “The attacks happen dozens of times a day. Dozens of cars, utility buildings, residential buildings, administrative buildings, and garages have been hit; they’re just setting everything on fire,” Rybakova, who serves as a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd mechanized brigade and is based in Kramatorsk, told CNN on Monday. “Toward the evening and in the morning, almost no one is out and about,” she said. “During the day, there are gunmen everywhere … everyone walks around with a rifle, goes out for a coffee with a rifle, heads to the store with a rifle and so on because drones are everywhere now and you never know. They can strike at any moment.” As the first visit to Kyiv by US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner came and went Sunday without a major breakthrough, Ukraine is increasingly finding itself on the backfoot in many spots along the eastern front line. It’s a major change in fortune compared to the spring, when Kyiv was liberating more land than it was losing. Jennie Olmsted, a Russia analyst at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a US-based conflict monitor, said that while a quick breakthrough is unlikely, the situation has shifted in Moscow’s favor. “(The Russians) are conducting continued infiltration missions and are slowly making progress towards Sloviansk and Kramatorsk and are advancing in Kostyantynivka, but at a really slow pace,” she said. Russia advanced or infiltrated into about 124 square kilometers (47.8 square miles) of Ukraine’s territory in August, roughly a quarter of the amount of terrain it seized in the same month last year, according to ISW. This is a glacial pace, and it comes at a massive cost to Moscow. Western intelligence services estimate Russia is losing some 40,000 troops a month – a rate of roughly 340 casualties for every square kilometer. But unfortunately for Ukraine, Russia is chipping away at the so-called “fortress belt” in the east, a string of four industrial cities that form the backbone of Ukraine’s eastern defenses. The belt is key for defending what remains of the Donbas region, but also for the rest of eastern and central Ukraine. The topography and the population centers, with the roads and railroads that connect them, create a natural barrier before the less defensible, sparsely populated flat plains to the west. The concern is that if Russia were to break through here, it could then advance deeper into Ukraine at a much faster pace. That’s why Ukraine has spent the last few years pouring resources into fortifying the cities that form this defensive line: Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka and Kostyantynivka. The fortress belt has slowly eroded over the past four and a half years. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka, has now been effectively lost as a stronghold. The Russians have spent almost a year trying to seize it and, while pockets of Ukrainian resistance remain in the north of the city, any operational value for Kyiv is long gone. It’s a recurring theme along the front lines. The Russian military cannot take over cities and towns in a quick offensive that leaves most of the infrastructure intact. Instead, Moscow wages slow, grinding warfare that renders them uninhabitable. It took Russian forces nine months of fighting to seize the nearby city of Bakhmut and nearly two years to take Pokrovsk, another supply hub. By the time they managed to gain full control, the two cities were mostly destroyed – and their strategic value to Ukraine lost, Olmsted said. Even so, each small gain made by Russia carries major propaganda potential. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly made it clear, including over the weekend, that he is not willing to give up on his war goals in Ukraine, which include seizing all of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Russia already occupies about 81% of Donetsk and almost all of Luhansk. Moscow said in April that it had managed to seize the latter in its entirety, but Kyiv says it maintains some pockets of control. According to Kremlin aide and negotiator Yury Ushakov, Putin told Witkoff and Kushner that the Russian army was making “tangible advances” on the battlefield and that it would soon achieve its objectives there. CNN has been unable to verify the claim but it points to the importance of Russia’s information war. Putin has reportedly said he expects Russian forces to seize the remainder of the two regions by the end of the year (after his reported 14 previous deadlines to do so came and went). Laying the ground According to the Ukraine-controlled Donetsk regional military administration, nearly 93,000 Ukrainians, including more than 4,800 children, are still living in the areas that remain under Kyiv’s control. But life is becoming increasingly difficult there. Hennadiy Yudin, a police officer with the “White Angels,” a special unit which helps the military evacuate civilians from frontline villages, said it was now impossible for his officers to drive into the town of Dobropillya and neighboring villages. “The military are evacuating people on foot and our guys are picking them up about 10 kilometers from Dobropillya – that’s the closest we can get. Otherwise, evacuation is completely impossible there; the whole area is mined and the number of drones is just insane,” Yudin told CNN. Rybakova told CNN there are still many civilians living in Kramatorsk, although she said she expected the situation to change. “Life is still going on. (The authorities) haven’t imposed a curfew yet … this had a huge impact (in towns further to the east) – all the businesses started leaving. They say they’ll be imposing one soon,” she said. Kramatorsk has long served as a strategic rear point for the Ukrainian units serving along the eastern front lines – and as a place to which exhausted troops can retreat for a few days of rest before their next mission. But that is no longer an option. “There’s shelling here every day. Guided bombs, a massive barrage, eight at a time,” Rybakova said. “Just last night, they bombed the house where I used to live. We moved out of there a few months ago and it’s just completely destroyed there now.” As Russia continues to inch towards these cities, the remaining residents fear Moscow is laying the ground for a future attack. “They are setting conditions and preparing the battle space for offenses against Sloviansk,” Olmsted said. “They’re really trying to degrade Ukrainian logistics and defenses in the area, and they are making it difficult for Ukrainian forces to get logistics up to their forward positions, and in the city.”

articles.title: Toxic air after 9/11: Mamdani releases documents showing how New Yorkers were misled
articles.summary: US News: Days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, New York City has reportedly published a number of previously withheld records suggestin.
articles.body: Days before the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, New York City has reportedly published a number of previously withheld records suggesting officials misled the public about dangerous air quality in the aftermath of the atrocity.At a press conference on Tuesday, Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled some 170,000 pages relating to health concerns following the collapse of the Twin Towers, Al Jazeera reported.Mamdani said the release would finally bring "accountability" that New Yorkers had long been denied, arguing that "people got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air."Among the papers is the “Harding Memo”, which was sent in October 2001 to then-deputy mayor Robert Harding, which anticipated thousands of lawsuits over "toxic exposure" and set out ways the city might limit its liability.According to the BBC, the memo warned the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims, partly because health advisories had prompted people to return to the area too soon, risking "toxic exposure or emotional harm."A separate 2002 memo showed officials feared criticism from Congressman Jerry Nadler over asbestos levels could cause a public relations crisis. The BBC reported that this memo, attributed to adviser Ester Fuchs, referenced testimony from the city's health chief claiming no elevated indoor asbestos, even though dust samples showed low levels of the carcinogen.Residents were reportedly told to clean debris with "wet mops and rags," despite guidance that asbestos should only be handled by licensed professionals.Tuesday’s document release also resolves a litigation brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch. The group's director, Benjamin Chevat, said four mayoral administrations had withheld the truth for 25 years while insisting the air was "safe and acceptable".Comedian and long-time advocate Jon Stewart, who appeared alongside Mamdani, said the disclosure was essential even though it could not change past outcomes.According to reports, employees and residents were allowed to return to nearby buildings within weeks of the collapse, as thousands of police officers, construction workers, and firefighters worked in the soot, often reportedly without proper protection.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Surrey prisoners' artwork goes on display at Guildford Cathedral
articles.summary: The free exhibition, called Transformations, is at Guildford Cathedral until 19 October.
articles.body:
Artwork from prisoners inside HMP Coldingley in Surrey is being exhibited at Guildford Cathedral.

The free exhibition, called Transformations, started on Tuesday and was due to run until 19 October.

The Very Reverend Bob Cooper, Dean of Guildford, said: "The Transformations exhibition reminds us that every person has inherent dignity and the capacity for change.

"Art has a remarkable ability to open conversations, encourage reflection and inspire hope."

The cathedral is also hosting an event called Transformative Power of Art on 12 October which will bring together faith leaders, prison practitioners and charity representatives who will discuss how art can benefit those in prison.

"The evening will also provide an opportunity to engage with wider questions around justice, redemption, community and second chances, with perspectives from those working directly in prison ministry and rehabilitation," a spokesperson from the cathedral said.

articles.title: Family of Lindsay and Craig Foreman mark 600 day Iran detention
articles.summary: Lindsay and Craig Foreman, from East Sussex, are being held in Tehran after being detained in 2025.
articles.body:
The detention of a couple held in Iran "should shock people" as their time being held reaches over 600 days, their family says.

Family of Craig and Lindsay Foreman say the wait for the couple to be returned has been "an incredibly long time", after they were detained while on a motorbiking trip in Iran in January 2025.

The couple, from East Sussex, were sentenced to 10 years in jail over espionage charges, which they both deny, and are continuing to be held in Evin prison.

Lindsay's son, Joe Bennett, from Folkestone in Kent, said: "We are constantly knocking on every door available to us."

He added: "It's trying to get the right people to see this and start calling it what it is. We are 20 months down and it feels like we have taken a step back.

"It should shock people that they are still there and there hasn't been any sense of large progress."

A spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said the couple's health and welfare is "a top priority", and that it is "working to provide consular assistance".

Craig and Lindsay Foreman have been held since January 2025, and were sentenced in February 2026. Wednesday, 9 September will mark 614 days since they were detained, Bennett said.

The couple's family spoke to them at the end of August , the first time in three months they had been able to talk, but have not been able to since.

Family and friends will be marking the milestone of their detention by joining a motorbike ride in London, greeting MPs as they arrive for Prime Minister's Questions and delivering a letter to the Iranian embassy.

Bennett said being able to have another call with his mother and Craig would "mean the world", and is one of the things he is calling for in his letter to the Iranian embassy.

Craig and Lindsay's family met Middle East minister Stephen Doughty in August who "set out how unjustified and appalling we consider their incarceration to be, and the action that the UK Government is taking to try and secure their release", an FCDO spokesperson said.

Bennett had previously called for a prisoner exchange in order to ensure their release, and has urged the FCDO and other bodies to help bring the couple back to the UK.

articles.title: Worcester uni awards singer Toyah Willcox honorary doctorate
articles.summary: Birmingham-born Toyah Willcox says she is "so proud" to receive an honorary doctorate.
articles.body:
Singer-songwriter Toyah Willcox has been awarded an honorary doctorate by the University of Worcester.

During a career spanning more than four decades, Willcox recorded 25 albums, achieved 13 Top 40 singles, appeared in more than 20 feature films and over 40 stage productions.

Alongside her artistic achievements, she has been a patron of the Avon Navigation Trust since 2024, supporting environmental education and youth programmes.

Speaking at the ceremony at Worcester Cathedral on Tuesday, she said: "I'm so proud and it's such an honour to be asked by Worcester University because I live within this area."

She added: "The area means everything to me. My friends [and] my family all love Worcester and where I live.

The Birmingham-born singer, who now lives in Pershore, said she had been "very surprised in a very pleasant way" to open the letter confirming her honorary title.

"It's fabulous to have this and to be seen and heard."

But she said she felt "pretty terrified" to address the students at their graduation.

"There's a huge gap in age between me and these students," Willcox said.

"I'm 68, they will be around the age of 20, and everything that influenced me is not in their sphere.

"So I wanted to talk to them in a way that I thought would help them, but it's about communication, it's about kindness, it's about friendship, it's about revision and always learning.

"I tried to find stories from my past that I know will resonate with them when they step into the outside world."

One of the artist's main messages was the importance of networking and creating contacts in a specific industry.

She said: "It's so important to be... I hate to say it, but gregarious, because some people are really shy.

"But... letting people know you are a good supportive friend, that you can be part of a team and you're brilliant in an ensemble - that will bring you so much work. "

Other notable names to receive an honorary doctorate in Worcester, include journalist Helen Lewis, internationally-renowned historian Prof Dame Linda Colley, and sports stars Dawn Scott and Lark Atkin-Davies.

About 2,500 students are expected to graduate during three days of ceremonies, celebrating achievements across subjects including health, education, business, science, humanities, sport and the arts.

articles.title: Nature GCSE backers say more 'greenlightenment' is needed
articles.summary: Steve Backshall calls for nature education as a survey says 55% of children have not climbed a tree.
articles.body:
Naturalist Steve Backshall and Lost Gardens of Heligan co-founder Sir Tim Smit have called for more "greenlightenment" to put nature education at the heart of school curriculums.

It comes as the government has been consulting on a new natural history GCSE , which Sir Tim said was a "seismic moment for British education", adding "a deep understanding of the natural world is fundamental to humanity's future".

Backshall, who hosted the Wild Heligan experience to excite young people about wildlife, said: "I see every day how nature revitalises, restores and fills people with joy."

A survey by Heligan of 1,004 parent and child groups across England found 55% of children had never climbed a tree.

Backshall said: "We can get so much from the wild world, but now more than ever the wild world needs us.

"Young people who are engaged with nature will be happier, healthier and more likely to take on our planet's problems."

Sir Tim said: "It is our responsibility to equip the next generation with the tools to protect nature so it doesn't become history."

He added children had not lost their interest in nature but had lost opportunities to experience it.

The survey found "ordinary contact with nature" was unfamiliar to many children and 61% of children had never collected a conker or camped in a tent.

The research also found 34% of children they asked said they would definitely choose the proposed natural history GCSE if their school offered it, with another 41% saying they probably would.

The government said, if brought in, the GCSE would "ensure that children are equipped with the highly sought after skills for the workforce of a changing world" and could help reduce the number of number of young people not in education, employment or training.

articles.title: Funeral for PC Matthew Blades killed in Middlesbrough A66 crash
articles.summary: PC Matthew Blades' family say he brought light and laughter into every room.
articles.body:
The funeral of one of the two police officers killed in a wrong-way crash is to take place later.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

Road closures will be in place in Hartlepool for PC Blades' funeral from 07:30 BST to allow for a full police ceremonial funeral.

Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.

Somerville said flowers had been delivered to the force's stations and people from Australia, France and America had been in touch.

"The support has been overwhelming, and it's been comforting," she said.

Somerville added even small acknowledgements of respect from the public, such as a nod or a thank you when they see police out and about, had brought officers "so much strength".

Officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned onto the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

PC Blades and PC Clough were in a vehicle looking for the Passat after its cloned registration plates triggered an automated number plate recognition camera, although they were not involved in the pursuit, according to the IOPC.

Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Cahill and Jakub Matusiak also died in the crash.

Hutton Avenue in Hartlepool will be closed from the junction with Mulgrave Road, alongside St Paul's Road and South Road from the junction with Mitchell Street.

Vehicles still parked on these roads after 07:30 BST will be removed.

Somerville said: "All of the officers across the country will have felt this and Cleveland is such a small force, so it's personal to have lost Matthew and Tom.

"I think the common feeling has been a sense of duty and a sense of pride, doing everything we can to make it perfect."

The force federation chair said Cleveland officers would be standing side-by-side in uniform at the funeral "filled with pride and dignity".

"I've spoken to Matthew's family and he was described as a best friend, a husband, a father, a brother and a son," Somerville said.

"He was funny and his laughter and silly jokes made them smile even when they least expected it, he brought light and laughter into every room he came into.

"And life feels unbearably quiet without him now."

PC Blades taught English at Carmel College in Darlington before joining the police force.

The school remembered him as an "intelligent, kind and approachable teacher" who "gave generously of himself to the young people in his care".

articles.title: Douglas Head officially designated a conservation area
articles.summary: Douglas Head has been formally designated a Conservation Area - but what does that actually mean?
articles.body:
Douglas Head has been formally designated a Conservation Area by the Manx government.

Douglas City Council said it "welcomed" the move, recognising the headland's "significant historical, architectural and cultural importance".

It follows years of campaigning by local historians and two public consultations, the most recent of which found 92% support for the move.

While the designation does not prevent all development on the headland, it does restrict the kind of changes owners to property within the boundary can make without first obtaining planning permission.

This includes for things like replacing windows or altering roofs.

Applications consider whether any alterations would preserve or enhance the area's character.

The Isle of Man's Area Plan says applications within the boundary "will generally not be supported."

Douglas Head already has eight registered buildings, more than almost anywhere else on the island outside of central Douglas.

They include the Great Union Camera Obscura (1892), Douglas Lighthouse, the Harbour Swing Bridge Tower and its original 1895 machinery, and Harold Tower.

articles.title: Gloucestershire beaver release 'could help fight drought issues'
articles.summary: Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust is looking for suitable areas to reintroduce the animals.
articles.body:
Supporters of a plan to reintroduce beavers to a county say they could help landscapes become more resilient to drought and climate change.

Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust and Forestry England are surveying different parts of the county to assess their suitability for a new reintroduction programme.

"Beavers are a keystone species" said Emily Bowen of the Beaver Trust. "They are ecosystem engineers, which means that they can have a massive impact on the landscape around them."

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which would have to approve the measure, said it could make a "huge difference to nature recovery".

Teen given life sentence for murdering man in alley

'We raised £26k in a week to fight developers'

Nurse said dementia patient 'didn't need birthday cake'

"By changing the land to suit their needs, they can change it in such a way that boosts biodiversity and increases resilience in terms of climate change," Bowen added.

As semi-aquatic mammals, beavers are known for building dams that create ponds and wetlands.

Even small streams can feed a substantial wetland habitat that will then support an abundant array of biodiversity.

Beavers are a native species, but have not been a regular sight in the west of England for around 400 years, after hunting for food and medical ingredients forced their numbers to dramatically decline.

A Defra spokesperson said: "Reintroducing beavers has the potential to make a huge difference to nature recovery, and we are proud to champion this work.

"We will continue to support our partners and ensure that the return of beavers benefits both wildlife and communities."

Beavers have already been living at Greathough Brook in the Forest of Dean since 2018 and regular surveys have revealed a dramatic increase in biodiversity.

"I've seen stoats, I've seen weasels, I've even seen pine martens," said Kate Wollen, from Forestry England.

"The beavers have created this amazing habitat that has brought in all the insects that are at the bottom of the food chain and then it brings in all the other animals that then feed on them, it's just a whole wonderful network of habitats."

A new re-introduction programme in the Severn Vale area would require a government licence.

Studies are being carried out to find suitable locations and a consultation is underway with landowners and users who might be affected by the change in the landscape.

"We have to make sure that we are working really closely with people who live, work and manage the areas that we're thinking about putting beavers," said Mega Adamou, of Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust.

"We'll be seeing more complex wetland habitats being created," she added.

"We'll be seeing a little bit more resilience to drought in those areas where the beavers might end up living."

"It's been really interesting to see how the general public have taken to beavers and getting people thinking about seeing them back in our countryside."

There have been three licensed releases of beavers in England to date, with about 100 animals expected to be released this year.

articles.title: Israel’s war leaves Lebanon’s schools balancing students and the displaced
articles.summary: Schools in Lebanon are set to start on September 15, but many still host people displaced by Israel’s war.
articles.body:
Froun, Lebanon, a village devastated by Israeli air strikes, is preparing to reopen its school for students while still providing shelter for displaced people.

Israel's intensified war on Lebanon led to the displacement of over one million Lebanese, with Froun included in a pilot zone programme despite never being under Israeli control.

Lebanon faces challenges in reopening schools due to extensive damage from conflict, with over 340 schools damaged and 454 affected by displacement-related disruption.

Froun, Lebanon – Abbas Makki is the principal of a school in the village of Froun, in southern Lebanon. He sits behind the desk in his office, preparing for the return of students to his school, which is also doubling as a centre for displaced people in the village.

Froun is littered with rubble from buildings destroyed by Israeli air strikes. Local officials say most of the village still has no state-provided water or electricity. This means that as the return to the school year approaches in Lebanon, many of the displaced are unable to return home.

"Our area has been devastated," Makki said. He noted that the school reopened on the first day after a US-declared June truce was announced between Lebanon and Israel. And now, after the summer break, it will reopen again – but continue to provide shelter for those in need.

"We will reopen the school [for students], but will not abandon the displaced people," Makki said.

Israel's war on Lebanon intensified for the second time in two years in March. Two days after Israeli and US attacks killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah responded by attacking Israel for the first time in more than a year.

The Israeli response to those strikes was devastating. The Israeli military re-invaded southern Lebanon – after largely pulling out in early 2025 – and forced the displacement of more than one million Lebanese, mostly from southern Lebanon, the Bekaa Valley in the east, and Beirut's southern suburbs.

In April, US-brokered direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon began, despite Hezbollah's preference for indirect talks. In late June, a framework agreement was reached between the two sides, including "pilot zones" where Israel would pull out its troops and the Lebanese Army would enter to disarm Hezbollah.

Froun, a town in the Bint Jbeil district about two hours' drive south of Beirut, was one of three villages included in the pilot zone programme, despite local residents saying that Israel had never taken control of the town.

Still, shortly after the framework agreement was announced, locals who had fled the fighting in the area started returning to the town, only to find piles of concrete rubble where their homes once stood. Some, like Soujoud Ramadan, have taken to living at the local school.

Ramadan now runs a small market by the entrance to the school, where she sells snacks and basic household necessities. She said she opened the market here because the town centre and its surrounding areas had been destroyed, forcing residents who need to visit a shop to travel by car to villages with less destruction.

"We returned here after the ceasefire to a completely destroyed village," she said. "But I hope Froun will return like it was and even better."

The public school year is set to start on Tuesday, September 15 in Lebanon. A local official told Al Jazeera that the Lebanese government had also set that day as a goal for restoring water and electricity to Froun.

Since the establishment of the framework agreement, many Lebanese sheltering in schools have returned to their homes, or found other accommodation.

But Israel's attacks on southern Lebanon in recent days have driven some back from their homes. On Monday, Israel killed 12 people in southern Lebanon, including two children, after it hit a residential building and a car in the Nabatieh region's Kfar Reman. According to Lebanon's Ministry of Health, 4,381 people in Lebanon have been killed by Israel since March 2.

Today, hundreds of thousands of people are still displaced in Lebanon.

"A school cannot function simultaneously as a proper shelter and a normal learning environment," said Maysoun Chehab, the senior education programme specialist in the Beirut office of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). "Where schools continue to accommodate displaced families, reopening will inevitably be delayed or classroom capacity reduced. The solution cannot simply be to evacuate families; dignified and safe alternative accommodation must first be secured."

On September 2, Lebanon's Education Minister Rima Karami said that every student would have access to schools for the 2026-27 academic year, and said public schools would have in-person classes wherever possible.

But during a tour of southern Lebanon, Karami noted that no displaced person sheltering in a school would be removed "without an alternative being offered".

In Srifa, a town near Froun, local media reported that displaced people had been moved from the town's public school to a local private school. And in Bourj Qalaway, just to the south, Lebanon's Council of the South has reportedly planned to install 17 prefabricated classrooms where the village's school used to be before it was destroyed in Israel's attacks.

In Froun, Makki said prefabricated houses would be provided for the displaced to allow students to go back to school.

"The important thing is that we will not mistreat the people nor will we stop classes," he said.

Even with efforts from the government and locals to reopen schools, educational experts said the new school year would be a massive challenge after the widespread damage to southern Lebanon.

"Lebanon is not facing a normal school reopening; it is trying to protect education amid continued hostilities, displacement and extensive damage to schools," Chehab told Al Jazeera.

She added that more than 340 schools have been damaged and 454 have been affected by conflict or displacement-related disruption.

"The immediate challenge is to rehabilitate schools and replace lost equipment, but the deeper challenge is to prevent a generation from paying the price of the conflict," she said.

Students in Lebanon have had their school years disrupted for each of the last seven years, creating a lost generation of students .

"Education cannot wait for complete political or security stability," Chehab said. "Every effort must be made now to return children to safe learning, support their teachers and restore a sense of normality and hope. Protecting education today means protecting Lebanon's human capital, social cohesion and future."

articles.title: Why US-Iran war over Hormuz is threatening the Gulf’s waters
articles.summary: US-Iran attacks on tankers around Hormuz are raising fears of devastating oil spills across the Gulf.
articles.body:
The United States-Iran war is increasingly being fought at sea, with both sides targeting oil tankers and other vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

On September 8, the US struck five Iranian oil tankers, provoking an Iranian attack on Jordan’s Al-Azraq airbase.

Just three days earlier, the US also hit three other Iranian tankers. Those strikes came after Iran launched ballistic missiles towards a US aircraft carrier and a navy destroyer near the Strait, according to US Central Command. Iran too subsequently said it had targeted three oil tankers travelling through what it called an “unauthorised route” in the Strait, as well as three US-linked vessels elsewhere.

The tit-for-tat attacks have turned Hormuz into a potential environmental tinderbox. With tankers carrying millions of barrels of crude and petroleum products passing through or waiting around the waterway, a successful strike could trigger a fire, a sinking – or a major oil spill.

As of September 7, MarineTraffic data shows 42 tankers waiting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, while hundreds of other vessels are waiting or moving slowly in the wider Gulf of Oman and Gulf region. Of those tankers, 18 are carrying oil.

While it is not known exactly how much — if any — crude they were carrying, these vessels have an estimated combined capacity to carry 1.76 million cubic metres of oil and petroleum products – cargo that could be at risk if attacks on commercial shipping continue.

That — 1.76 million cubic metres of crude oil — is roughly 11.1 million barrels of oil, and is equivalent to about 11 percent of the world’s daily oil demand.

It is also enough oil to fill roughly 714 Olympic-sized swimming pools.

Now imagine the environmental damage. A major tanker strike or sinking could release millions of litres of oil into the Gulf – potentially contaminating coastlines, fisheries and fragile marine ecosystems.

And unlike an oil spill on land, oil at sea can spread over a vast area, carried by currents and winds far from the original site of the accident.

How many ships have been hit in recent days?

On September 5, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces struck three Iranian crude-oil tankers — one off Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil-export hub; another near Jask; and a third, an unladen tanker, in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was ordered to abandon ship.

The strikes marked a new escalation in attacks on oil shipping in the region.

Since the start of the war, at least 75 ships have been attacked, with at least 21 seafarers killed. Of those vessels, two incidents have resulted in minor oil spills, while six have caused fires.

Oil has been leaking from the Caroline Bezengi since it ran aground about 22 nautical miles (41km) off Oman after its crew reported a suspected explosion in early June. Reuters estimates the tanker was carrying 800,000 barrels of oil.

Oman’s Environment Authority warned that the spill could affect about 40km (25 miles) of coastline near Ras Madraka, as well as Masirah Island.

On August 3, the Minoan Pioneer, a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier, was struck by an unidentified projectile off Oman and caught fire.

Satellite imagery taken on August 10 showed a large slick near Qeshm Island, while another slick was detected near Sirri Island. Experts said the Qeshm slick likely came from the Minoan Pioneer, but could not independently confirm its source.

What is the impact of tankers being attacked on marine life?

Past conflicts like Operation Desert Storm — in which the US fought Iraq after Saddam Hussein’s forces had invaded Kuwait — also left a legacy of environmental pollution.

As Iraqi forces retreated they set Kuwaiti oil wells on fire. These burned for months, and unleashed millions of gallons of oil into the northern Gulf coast which damaged Kuwaiti and Saudi Arabian coastlines for decades.

Over 770km of coastline from southern Kuwait to Abu Ali Island in Saudi Arabia were engulfed in oil and tar, wiping out the local marine ecosystems.

The damage from the oil spill was colossal and destroyed coastline sediments, marine species and ecosystems.

Thirty five years later, the US-Israel war on Iran has once again imperilled the fragile marine ecosystem. US airstrikes have pounded Iranian vessels and oil tankers near the Iranian coast line. Iran has retaliated with similar strikes against ships and tankers from other countries.

The Gulf contains resilient coral reefs and mangrove forests that survive in one of the world’s hottest and most saline marine environments.

The enclosed water is a shallow, semi-enclosed sea supporting coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, mudflats and salt marshes.

These habitats are critical feeding and nursery grounds for fish, turtles, dugongs and migratory birds, while supporting fisheries and protecting coastlines.

With limited water exchange with the wider Indian Ocean, pollution can place added pressure on the Gulf’s marine ecosystems.

A study by the University of South Florida in June stated that based on satellite imagery, the oil spills in Gulf and Strait of Hormuz were four times as much in March than the year before.

The research team noted high instances of oil leaks from vessels trapped in the strait and around trapped vessels.

Oil spills lay on top of the water, and damage and poison marine life, pollute the water, and smother coral reefs and mangroves.

Dr. Hussein Samh al Masroori, Associate Professor at Sultan Qaboos University, speaking to Al Jazeera says that oil and petroleum hydrocarbons can directly affect fish, corals, plankton and other marine organisms. Fish eggs and larvae can be particularly vulnerable.

“Sensitive habitats such as coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds and coastal sediments may retain pollutants for much longer,” he says. “There can also be indirect effects through changes in water quality, food-web productivity, fish distribution and potentially spawning or migration patterns. For fisheries, this can translate into reduced fishing opportunities, higher costs and loss of income for coastal communities.”

Oil can also become trapped in sediments, covering beach sand and mud – like in the case of the 1991 oil spill off the Gulf.

Oil spills can smother other marine life, from microscopic plankton and fish larvae to coral reefs, seagrass and mangroves.

The Gulf countries primarily rely on desalination as the primary source of water for the entirety of its nearly 65 million population. Iran also has several desalination plants along its southern coast, some of which have come under attack by the US. There are approximately 15 million people living along the coast of Iran.

Al Masoori explains further that oil contamination near seawater intakes can affect raw-water quality, interfere with treatment processes and, in severe situations, require temporary operational restrictions.

“The actual risk depends greatly on the location of the spill, currents, distance and depth of the intake, and treatment technology.” says al Masroori.

He adds that modern monitoring, modelling and advanced treatment systems can substantially reduce the risk. The priority is early detection so contaminated water can be prevented from entering desalination systems.

articles.title: New Hampshire primary results: Key takeaways for US midterm elections
articles.summary: The GOP aims to gain a New England foothold as Democrats strive to retain the Senate seat.
articles.body:
Republican John E Sununu and Democrat Chris Pappas have won their primary elections in New Hampshire and will compete for a United States Senate seat that could flip the chamber in November.

Former Senator Sununu and House Representative Pappas are battling to replace outgoing Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen. Both candidates were strong frontrunners in their respective races.

In the House Republican primaries, Anthony DiLorenzo won in the 1st Congressional District and Lily Tang Williams won the 2nd District without much contest.

Tang Williams will face House Representative Maggie Goodlander, who is running for a second term. Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, defeated retired Marine Maura Sullivan in a tight Democratic primary for the 1st District.

Republican Kelly Ayotte dominated the state gubernatorial race, defeating two little-known challengers. Former US senator and state attorney general Ayotte is seeking a second two-year term, running against Cinde Warmington, who ran unopposed for the Democratic nomination.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state in the 2024 presidential election by a margin of 2.78 percentage points over President Donald Trump.

While New Hampshire has largely elected Republicans for state government and Democrats for Congress, the Grand Old Party views the race as an opportunity to gain a foothold in New England.

Democrats hope to retain the seat, as they need a net gain of four seats to retake the Senate currently controlled by Republicans.

The second frontrunner in the Democratic primary race, democratic socialist Karishma Manzur, failed to defeat Pappas despite gaining on him in recent weeks. Manzur criticised Pappas for his relationship with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

Sununu defeated seven opponents, including a former state senator from Massachusetts, Scott Brown.

“Chris Pappas has three main qualities: ineffective, partisan and out of touch with New Hampshire,” Sununu said at a victory party.

Pappas sought to tie Sununu to the increasingly unpopular US President Donald Trump during his campaign. Trump endorsed Sununu, despite the Republican candidate describing him as a “loser” during the 2024 presidential race.

“While New Hampshire families are struggling to make ends meet, John Sununu has thrown his lot in with Donald Trump and supports the policies that cater to big corporations and billionaires while they make life harder for Granite Staters,” Pappas said.

Tight contest for Democratic House nomination

Stefany Shaheen won the Democratic nomination for the 1st District and will compete for the seat left open by Pappas.

In the 2nd Congressional District, Democratic incumbent Goodlander defeated progressive challenger Paige Beauchemin. Tang Williams won the Republican primary in her third attempt for the seat and was the GOP nominee in the 2024 elections.

Meanwhile, political newcomer DiLorenzo defeated three other candidates without much difficulty, having received an endorsement from Trump.

Voters across Rhode Island head to the polls tomorrow. Its most closely watched election is the race for governor.

Governor Dan McKee, facing voter dissatisfaction and low job approval ratings, is up against challenger Helena Foulkes, who challenged him in the 2022 gubernatorial primary elections. Foulkes has led in polls by double digits for months.

Harris won Rhode Island in the 2024 presidential election with a lead of 13.7 percentage points.
